title: Learning from Mistakes
keyIdea: A mistake shows you exactly what to learn next, but only if you look at it before you rub it out. Find the step that went wrong, then ask why: was it a slip (you knew it but rushed), a misconception (you had the wrong idea) or a misread (you missed what the question asked)? Each kind needs a different fix. A mistake that keeps coming back is the one to practise first. Mistakes you were sure about are often remembered best once you see why.

kid: Everyone gets things wrong. Mistakes are not bad news. They show you what to learn next. But only if you look at them first, before you rub them out.
Go through your work line by line. Find the line where it went wrong. Then ask: why did it go wrong?

There are three main kinds. A slip is when you knew it but rushed. A misconception is when you had the wrong idea. A misread is when you missed what the question asked. A slip needs a slow check. A wrong idea needs to be learned again. A misread needs you to read the question again.
Look for the mistake that keeps coming back. Practise that one first. Then try a new question to check the fix has stuck. Spot it, find why, fix it, try again.
adult: Learning from mistakes is error analysis, a core part of metacognition: thinking about your own thinking. The Education Endowment Foundation's guidance on metacognition and self-regulated learning advises teaching children to plan, monitor and evaluate their work, and to treat errors as information. Hattie's Visible Learning research ranks feedback among the strongest influences on learning, and feedback is most useful when the learner acts on it.

Key terms: error analysis, slip (a careless error on something the child knows), misconception (a wrong idea held with belief, such as thinking 0.25 is bigger than 0.5), misread (missing what the question asked), feedback and correction. Research by Butterfield and Metcalfe found the hypercorrection effect. Errors made with high confidence are more likely to be fixed for good once the right answer is shown. Surprise helps the correction stick.

Common mistakes: rubbing out or hiding wrong work before looking at it, treating all errors as carelessness, so misconceptions are never fixed, and redoing everything instead of the one error that repeats. Children also read a mistake as proof they are not clever. A common adult slip is to give the right answer at once; asking "Which line went wrong?" first teaches the child to find it.

In the lab your child taps the wrong line in three worked answers, sorts mistakes into slips, misconceptions and misreads, opens a marked test to find the error that keeps coming back, puts the four moves (spot it, find why, fix it, try a new one) in order, and sorts thoughts that help learning from ones that stop it.

familyTip: When homework comes back with crosses, sit together and pick one: "Which line went wrong? Was it a slip, a wrong idea or a misread?" Praise the finding, not just the fixing. Share one mistake of your own each week and what you learned from it.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tap the wrong line, sort slips, misconceptions and misreads, find the mistake that repeats, order the four moves, sort helpful thoughts.

practice.prompt: Sam knows 9 × 3 = 27 but wrote 28 because he was rushing. What kind of mistake is that?
practice.hint: Did Sam know the fact? What made it go wrong?
practice.explain: Sam knows the fact, so it is not a wrong idea. Rushing caused it, so it is a slip. A slow check would catch it.

practice.prompt: Ava got {n} sums wrong. {k} of them were because she forgot to carry. How many were for other reasons?
practice.hint: Take the carrying mistakes away from all the mistakes.
practice.explain: {n} − {k} = {=n-k} were for other reasons. Carrying caused {k}, so that is a good one to practise.

practice.prompt: Before you rub out a wrong answer, what should you do?
choices: Find the line that went wrong
practice.hint: Which move comes first: spot it, find why, fix it, or try again?
practice.explain: Spot it first. Finding the line that went wrong shows you exactly what to fix.

practice.prompt: Kit had {a} slips and {b} misreads on a test. How many mistakes is that?
practice.hint: Add the slips and the misreads together.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} mistakes. Slips need a slow check, and misreads need a careful read of the question.

pool.prompt: Ben thinks heavy things always sink. What kind of mistake is that?
pool.hint: Does Ben really believe it, or did he rush?
pool.explain: Ben believes a wrong idea, so it is a misconception. A big wooden log is heavy but floats.

pool.prompt: The question asked "How many are left?" Jo added the numbers. What kind of mistake?
pool.hint: Did Jo do what the question asked?
pool.explain: "How many are left" means take away. Jo missed the key words, so it is a misread.

pool.prompt: What are the four moves for learning from a mistake, in order?
choices: Spot it, find why, fix it, try a new one
Fix it, spot it, try a new one, find why
Rub it out, try a new one, spot it, fix it
pool.hint: You cannot fix it until you know why it went wrong.
pool.explain: First spot it, then find why, then fix it, then try a new question to check the fix has stuck.

pool.prompt: Mia's test had {n} mistakes. {k} came from the 7 times table. How many did not?
pool.hint: Take the 7 times table mistakes away.
pool.explain: {n} − {k} = {=n-k} did not. If {k} is the biggest group, the 7 times table is the one to practise first.

pool.prompt: Leo was sure the answer was 12, but it was 21. He sees why. What usually happens next time?
choices: He is more likely to remember the right answer
He is sure to get it wrong again
pool.hint: Think about how surprise helps you remember.
pool.explain: Being sure and wrong is a surprise. Surprise helps the right answer stick. Scientists call it the hypercorrection effect.

pool.prompt: Raj forgot to carry in {k} sums on Monday. After practising, he forgot in 1 sum on Friday. How many fewer carrying mistakes?
pool.hint: Take Friday's mistakes away from Monday's.
pool.explain: {k} − 1 = {=k-1} fewer mistakes. Practising the mistake that kept coming back worked.

pool.prompt: Ella thinks, "I got it wrong, so I'm stupid." Which thought helps her learn?
choices: "I'll hide it so no one sees"
pool.hint: Which thought leads to finding the cause?
pool.explain: Asking which step went wrong is error analysis. It shows what to fix. The other thoughts stop learning.

pool.prompt: Jo thinks 0.25 is bigger than 0.5 because 25 is bigger than 5. What will fix it?
choices: Learn again what tenths and hundredths mean
pool.hint: Is it a slip, a misconception or a misread?
pool.explain: It is a misconception, so the idea must be relearned. 0.5 is 5 tenths, which is 50 hundredths, more than 25 hundredths.
